def: Imprisonment by a military commander’s order, without charge or trial. In the West Bank it rests on sections 284–294 of Military Order 1651. Each order runs up to six months and can be renewed with no limit.
The classified material on which an administrative detention order is approved. Most of it is withheld from the detainee and the lawyer, so neither can answer it.
The consolidated Order regarding Security Provisions that governs arrest, trial and administrative detention of Palestinians in the West Bank.
Custody before a verdict: under interrogation, after an indictment, or during trial. HaMoked’s monthly figures count these people as one group.
The Israeli army courts, such as the one at Ofer, where Palestinians from the West Bank are tried. An internal army document reported a 99.74% conviction rate in 2010.

A status under the Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law (2002), which allows prolonged detention without trial with fewer safeguards than administrative detention. Most people held from Gaza are held under it.
A petition asking a court to order the state to say where a person is held. HaMoked filed 114 for people taken from Gaza; 38 were never located.

Visits by the International Committee of the Red Cross to people held. Israel stopped informing the ICRC about Palestinian detainees after 7 October 2023; the High Court ordered cooperation to resume on 3 June 2026.
The Israeli Supreme Court sitting as a court of first instance on petitions against the state. Petitions carry a number such as HCJ 76360-04-26.
A law passed 62–48 on 30 March 2026. In West Bank military courts it makes death the sentence in most convictions for deadly attacks, by simple majority, and the commander can no longer commute it.
The part of the West Bank under full Israeli control, where the Civil Administration rejects about 95% of Palestinian building applications.
An order to destroy a building put up without an Israeli permit. In 2026, permit demolitions displaced about 1,790 people in the West Bank by 19 October, 668 of them in East Jerusalem.
Land the army declares closed for training. Communities inside, such as those of Masafer Yatta in Firing Zone 918, face repeated demolition and eviction.
Binding orders the International Court of Justice issues while a case is pending. In South Africa v. Israel they were ordered on 26 January 2024 and extended in March and May 2024.
The ICJ’s answer to a legal question from the UN. On 19 July 2024 it found Israel’s continued presence in the occupied territory unlawful.
